threads.thread_goal: Align on current issues and approve target workflow scope

messages.text: Hi team, let's kick off the standardisation project. I'd like to understand what's causing the most friction in our front-of-house right now. Can everyone share their top pain points? We need to map out what T1 should cover—the current workflow from customer arrival through to handover. What should we prioritise?

Good question. From my side, the biggest issue is inconsistency in how we handle prescription requests. Some of us check expiry dates at different points, and I've seen near-misses where stock gets mixed up during busy periods. Also, the OTC section is a mess—customers can't find things and we end up spending time searching. I think we need clear steps for both prescription and OTC workflows, and we need to document the safety checks.

I agree with that. From the shelf filler perspective, I'm often unsure where things should go when we receive new stock. The layout isn't consistent, so I end up asking questions instead of just placing items. And the labels—some are old, some are missing. If we had a standard layout and clear labelling rules, I could work faster and more confidently.

I think the customer communication side is tricky too. When someone asks about a medicine or health question, I'm not always sure what I can say and what needs to go to the pharmacist. A quick guide would help. Also, I've noticed we don't always know if stock is in the right place or if it's expired.

Thanks for that clarity. So I'm hearing: (1) inconsistent prescription handling and safety checks, (2) OTC layout and findability, (3) shelf filler uncertainty on placement, (4) labelling gaps, and (5) customer communication boundaries. Let me propose we focus on these three first: prescription workflow consistency, standard shelf layout with clear labelling, and a daily verification checklist. Does that capture it?
Yes, that sounds right. I think we should also make sure the new workflow covers how we handle temperature-sensitive medicines. I've seen some items stored in the wrong place before.

I agree with those three priorities. For the prescription workflow, we need to document the exact steps—checking ID, verifying the prescription, checking stock, confirming with the customer, and handing over. And we need to make sure high-risk medicines are flagged. Should we include the near-miss reporting in the workflow too?

Good point. Yes, near-miss reporting should be part of the workflow. That ties into safety. So to confirm: we're standardising (1) prescription and OTC request handling with safety checks, (2) shelf layout and labelling, and (3) daily verification. T1 will document the current state and pain points, and we'll use that to design the new workflow. Does everyone agree on this scope?
Yes, that works for me. I'll help with the layout part once we have the workflow locked in.
Sounds good. When do we start on T1?

I'll start mapping the current workflow today and will share a draft by EOD tomorrow. I'll need input from at least two of you to validate it. 12454, can you review once I post? And 255566, I'll need your perspective on the shelf filler side.

threads.thread_goal: Define and approve the standard shelf layout and labelling rules

messages.text: I've drafted a standard shelf layout map for the pilot section. The idea is to group prescription-only medicines on the top shelf, OTC on the middle, and health products on the lower shelves. High-risk medicines like anticoagulants and antibiotics are clearly marked in red. Temperature-sensitive items have a separate cool zone. Can you all review A2 and let me know if this makes sense?

This looks good overall. I like the separation of high-risk items. One question: where are we putting the frequently requested OTC painkillers? They're in the middle shelf in your draft, but customers often ask for them first. Should they be more visible?
Good catch. I put them in the middle because they're high-volume, but you're right—visibility matters. Let me move them to eye level and keep the less common OTC items below. I'll update the map.

The layout is solid. Now, for the labelling rules—we need to be clear on what goes on each label. Font size, content, placement. I'm thinking we need A3 to cover: (1) what information must be on a medicine label, (2) what goes on a shelf label, (3) special rules for high-risk and temperature-sensitive items. Should we also include rules for changing labels when stock rotates?
Yes, the label rules are important. I've made mistakes before with old labels still on shelves. If we have clear rules about when to change them and how, that would help.

I agree. And for temperature-sensitive medicines, we need to make sure the label clearly indicates storage conditions. I've seen items stored at room temperature that should be refrigerated. The label should be obvious about that.

Exactly. So A3 needs to include storage condition icons or text that's hard to miss. I'll draft the labelling rules and include examples for high-risk and temperature-sensitive items. 12454, can you review for compliance? And 255566, I'll need your input on what's practical to implement during shelf filling.
The layout looks okay. I'm a bit confused about the temperature-sensitive section though. How will we know which items go there? Will there be a list?

Good question. Yes, we'll have a list as part of T11. It will show which medicines need refrigeration or cool storage, and the exact temperature range. That way, when you're shelving, you can check the list and place items correctly.

Alright, so here's what I'm proposing: we approve the updated shelf layout from 255566 as the pilot design, and we lock in the labelling rules once I've drafted A3. The layout and labels together will be our standard for the pilot section. Does that work?
Yes, I'm happy with that. Once we have A3, I can check it against our compliance requirements. And then we can move forward with T6—the pilot.
Agreed. I'll have the updated layout ready by tomorrow morning, and then I can start prepping the pilot section. Should I take before photos once I start?
Yes, please. Before and after photos are part of T6. That'll help us see the impact. I'll have A3 ready by EOD tomorrow as well.

threads.thread_goal: Lock in SOPs for stock reception and daily checks

messages.text: I've drafted the SOP for receiving and storing new stock. The steps are: (1) check delivery against order, (2) inspect for damage or expiry, (3) document any discrepancies, (4) store in correct location per the layout, (5) update stock system. I've also started a daily checklist for shelf fillers to verify stock levels, expiry dates, and label accuracy. Can you review A1 and A5?
The SOP looks clear. One thing—when we receive stock, sometimes the delivery is late or incomplete. Should we have a step for what to do if items are missing or delayed?

Good point. Yes, I'll add a step for handling discrepancies—if items are missing, we document it and notify the supplier. If items are damaged, we set them aside and report them. That's part of the documentation step.
The daily checklist is helpful. How long does it take to go through? I'm worried it might slow us down during busy shifts.

I've estimated about 15 minutes per aisle if you're thorough. The idea is to do it during quieter times—early morning or late afternoon. We can adjust the time estimate once we test it. That's part of T9.

This is solid. The SOP covers the key steps and the checklist is practical. I have one question: in the SOP, do we need to specify who can approve the storage of high-risk medicines? Should that always go to a pharmacist?
That's a good question. For high-risk medicines, I think we should have a pharmacist or senior assistant verify the placement. I'll add that to the SOP. It's a safety check.
I'm not sure I understand the checklist. Can you explain what 'label accuracy' means? Do we check if the label matches the medicine?

Yes, exactly. We check that the label on the shelf matches the medicine on the shelf, and that the label is legible and not damaged. We also check that the expiry date on the label is correct. I'll make that clearer in A5.

Good. So to confirm: we're approving the SOP for stock reception with the addition of pharmacist verification for high-risk items, and we're approving the daily checklist format. Both will be tested during the pilot. Does everyone agree?
Yes, I'm ready to use this during the pilot. I'll test the checklist and give feedback on timing.
Okay, I'll follow the SOP when we receive stock. Just remind me when we start.
I'll finalize A1 and A5 with the updates by tomorrow. Then we can roll them out as part of the training.

threads.thread_goal: Agree on training approach and rollout schedule

messages.text: Let's lock in the training approach and rollout schedule. I'm proposing: (1) a short training session for each person on the new workflow and layout, (2) a training checklist (A4) that each person signs off on, (3) a quick-reference guide for customer communication (A6), and (4) an implementation schedule (A8) that avoids peak hours. We have 21 days to roll out. What are our peak hours?
Peak hours are typically 9-11 AM and 4-6 PM on weekdays. Quietest times are 12-2 PM and after 6 PM. Weekends are busier overall. So we should schedule training and layout changes for the quiet slots.
That makes sense. For the shelf layout pilot, I can do the re-shelving during the 12-2 PM slot. How many days do you think it'll take?

For the pilot section, probably 2-3 hours if we're careful. So one quiet slot should be enough. Once we've tested it and refined, we can roll out to other sections. Now, for training—I'm thinking 30 minutes per person, covering the new SOP, layout, and checklist. Should we do it in small groups or one-on-one?
Small groups might be better. That way we can ask questions without holding up the whole team.
I agree. Small groups of 2-3 people. And we should do it during quiet times so we're not pulling people away from the counter. I can lead the training sessions if you want.

Perfect. So training format: small groups, 30 minutes, during quiet times, led by 12454. Each person signs off on A4 once they've completed training. For the customer communication guide (A6), I'll draft that based on common questions and compliance rules. And for the implementation schedule (A8), I'll map out which sections get the new layout and when, avoiding peak hours.
When will the training happen? I want to make sure I'm available.
I'll have the schedule ready by EOD tomorrow. It'll be in A8. We'll start training next week during the quiet slots.
What about the customer communication guide? Will that be part of the training?
Yes, A6 will be covered in training and then printed out for the counter. It'll be a one-page quick reference so you can check it if you're unsure about what to say to a customer.
I'm ready to lead the training. I'll make sure everyone understands the new workflow and can apply it. Should I also cover the near-miss reporting as part of training?

Yes, definitely. Near-miss reporting is part of the safety culture. I'll include it in A6 and you can cover it in training. Alright, so to confirm: training format is small groups, 30 minutes, during quiet times, led by 12454. Everyone signs off on A4. Implementation schedule avoids peak hours and is in A8. Does everyone agree?
Yes, that works for me.
Agreed. I'm ready to start the pilot once training is done.
Great. I'll have A4, A6, and A8 ready by EOD tomorrow. 12454, you'll have the training materials by then too. Let's aim to start training next week.

threads.thread_goal: Review pilot results, near-miss logs, and finalise follow-ups

messages.text: Pilot update: I've completed the re-shelving of the pilot section using the new layout. Before and after photos are attached. The layout is working well—items are easier to find and the high-risk medicines are clearly marked. I've been using the daily checklist for a week now, and it's taking about 12 minutes per aisle, which is faster than expected. No major issues so far.
That's great feedback. The faster checklist time is good news. Have you noticed any near-miss incidents or issues with the layout during the week?

One small issue: a customer picked up a temperature-sensitive medicine from the wrong shelf. The label was clear, but they didn't notice. I caught it before they left. I've logged it in the near-miss log (A7). It's a reminder that we need to make sure customers understand the layout too.

Good catch. That's exactly the kind of feedback we need. So the layout is solid, but we might need to add a visual cue or signage for temperature-sensitive items. Let me check the near-miss log and see if there are other patterns.

The new layout is definitely helping. I'm finding things faster and customers seem happier. The quick-reference guide (A6) is useful too—I've used it a few times when I wasn't sure about what to tell a customer.
That's good to hear. The guide is working as intended. Any feedback on the SOP for stock reception? Have you had any deliveries since we started?

Yes, we had a delivery yesterday. I followed the SOP and it went smoothly. The steps are clear and I didn't miss anything. The documentation part is a bit time-consuming, but it's important for safety.
I'm still getting used to the new layout, but it's better than before. I had one moment where I wasn't sure where to put a medicine, but I checked the layout map and found it. The training helped.
That's exactly what the layout map is for. Good that you checked. Any other questions or issues from anyone?

I've reviewed the near-miss log (A7) and there are only two entries so far—the one 255566 mentioned and one where a label was partially obscured. Both are minor and easily fixed. I think the pilot is successful. We should move forward with rolling out to the other sections.

Agreed. The pilot has validated the layout, the checklist, and the SOP. The near-miss log shows we're catching issues early. Now I need to summarize the outcomes and next steps. I'll draft a project summary (T12) that captures what we've learned and what still needs to be done. This will go to the pharmacist and store manager.
What's next for me? Should I start rolling out the layout to other sections?

Yes, but let's do it section by section. I'll update A8 with the rollout schedule for the remaining sections. We'll follow the same approach: re-shelf during quiet times, use the checklist, and log any issues. You'll lead the re-shelving for each section.
I'll help with the rollout too. And I'll continue monitoring the near-miss log and the daily checklist to make sure everything is working as expected.

Perfect. So the next steps are: (1) I'll finalize T12 with the project summary and outcomes, (2) 255566 will continue rolling out the layout section by section, (3) 12454 will monitor the near-miss log and checklist, and (4) everyone will continue following the new SOP and layout. We should have the full rollout done within the remaining time. Let me get T12 done by EOD tomorrow.
Sounds good. I'll keep following the SOP and using the checklist. Thanks for organizing this—it's definitely making things easier.
Yes, I'll keep using the layout and checklist. It's clearer now.
